chapter.name: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation
chapter.blurb: Early human history and evidence, human ancestors, Stone Age hunter-gatherers, the Neolithic revolution, the Sindhu-Sarasvati foundations and the Mesopotamian, Egyptian and Chinese civilisations.

scope_in.item: Why we study early human history; the invention of writing and early scripts
Human ancestors, tool making and movement out of Africa; fossils and tools as evidence
Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers and Mesolithic microlithic cultures in the subcontinent
The Neolithic revolution and the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods including Mehrgarh
Early Harappan foundations: crafts, farming, weights and measures and water management
The Mesopotamian civilisation: Sumerian, Akkadian, Assyrian and Babylonian city-states, cuneiform and the Code of Hammurabi
The Egyptian civilisation: Nile, calendar, hieroglyphs, pharaohs, pyramids and society
The Chinese civilisation and shared features of Bronze Age civilisations

scope_out.item: Detailed mature Harappan cities and their decline
Detailed religion and philosophy of these civilisations
Precise dating methods and archaeology techniques

concepts.name: Studying early human history and the invention of writing
concepts.description: Why we study early human history, how it is studied through archaeology, and the early writing systems and scripts.
concepts.idea: The time before writing is known mainly from archaeological evidence; writing marks the start of the historical period.
concepts.rule: Early human history is studied through tools, fossils and cave art. Biological evolution: australopithecines evolved into Homo sapiens. Cultural evolution: humans developed tools and techniques during the Quaternary Period. The Harappan script is undeciphered; cuneiform and hieroglyphs are deciphered and mark the historical period about 5000 years ago.
concepts.example: The Brahmi script was used from about 400 BCE and formalised by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.

questions.a: archaeological evidence

questions.q: The Harappan script has
questions.a: not yet been deciphered

questions.q: Which script was formalised by Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE?
questions.a: Brahmi

questions.q: Biological evolution refers to
questions.a: the gradual physical and genetic changes from early ancestors to modern humans
o: the gradual physical and genetic changes from early ancestors to modern humans
the invention of tools and their use in daily life
the growth of cities along the great rivers
the spread of farming from one region to another

questions.a: adapted to their surroundings by developing tools, techniques and technology
o: adapted to their surroundings by developing tools, techniques and technology
grew taller and stronger over many thousands of years
lost their tools and lived only by hunting with the hands
stopped using fire and lived only on raw food

questions.q: Cuneiform and hieroglyphs mark the beginning of the historical period about
questions.a: 5000 years ago

questions.q: Why are archaeological finds important for studying early humans?
questions.a: Written records do not exist for that time, so tools, bones and objects are the evidence
o: Written records do not exist for that time, so tools, bones and objects are the evidence
They replace all writing and make written records unnecessary
They are not used by historians, who depend only on books
They are found only in cities and tell us nothing of villages

questions.q: Why do we still not understand the Harappan script, while cuneiform is understood?
questions.a: The Harappan script, called Sindhu lipi, is pictographic and has not yet been deciphered, whereas cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs have been deciphered.

questions.q: Australopithecines are
questions.a: early human ancestors

questions.q: The Quaternary Period covers the last ____ lakh years, including the present.
From about 400 BCE the Brahmi script was used in
questions.a: parts of southern India and the Ganga Valley
o: parts of southern India and the Ganga Valley
Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and the Euphrates

questions.q: Name the two main kinds of change described as biological and cultural evolution.
questions.a: Biological evolution is the gradual physical and genetic change from australopithecines to Homo sapiens. Cultural evolution is how humans developed tools and technology to adapt to climate and environment.

questions.q: Name two early writing systems other than the Harappan script and where they were used.
questions.a: Cuneiform of the Sumerians in Mesopotamia and the hieroglyphic script of ancient Egypt.

questions.q: Explain how early human history is reconstructed without written records.
questions.a: Archaeologists study tools, bones, fossils and other objects left by early ancestors. Each clue helps them understand how people lived. Similar tools found in different places show groups using similar techniques, and excavations reveal what they created, used and depended on.
s: Says each clue tells how people lived
Mentions excavation or comparison of finds

questions.q: Why did the historical period begin at different times in different places?
questions.a: Written languages emerged at different times in different parts of the world
o: Written languages emerged at different times in different parts of the world
Because there was no time before writing in any place
Because all scripts were invented on the same day everywhere
Because the historical period began after the invention of iron

questions.q: What could historians learn if the Harappan script were deciphered?
questions.a: They could read the language and records of the Harappans, learning about their trade, administration, beliefs and society directly rather than only from objects.
s: Names a type of information such as trade or beliefs

questions.q: Explain the shift in human ways of life described in the chapter and why it mattered.
questions.a: Humans moved from hunting and gathering to agriculture and food production. The ability to produce surplus food and material goods laid the foundation for settled life, and later for cities and civilisation.
s: Led to settled life or civilisation

questions.q: Ravi says history begins only when writing begins, so earlier times are not part of history. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The period before writing is early human history, studied through archaeology. Writing marks the beginning of the historical period, but earlier times are still studied.
s: Says early history is studied through archaeology

questions.q: Suggest three questions an archaeologist would ask about a stone tool found at a site.
questions.a: What is it made of and how was it made? How old is it? What was it used for? Who used it and where did they live?
s: A question about material or making
A question about use or users

concepts.name: Early human ancestors and their movement out of Africa
concepts.description: The human ancestors, tool making, the movement out of Africa and the fossil and tool evidence.
concepts.idea: Our earliest ancestors evolved in Africa and spread across the Old World; making tools marks human behaviour.
concepts.rule: Earliest stone tools about 3.3 million years ago; hominins are tool makers. Homo habilis lived in Africa (Olduvai Gorge). Homo erectus, with handaxes and cleavers, first left Africa about 2 million years ago. Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago and moved out about 125,000 years ago.
concepts.example: Tools are called extra-corporal limbs because they extend what hands can do.

questions.q: Our earliest ancestors evolved and lived in
questions.a: Africa

questions.q: The first hominin to exit Africa was
questions.a: Homo erectus

questions.q: Homo habilis means "____ man".
questions.a: handy

questions.q: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about
questions.a: 300,000 years ago

questions.q: Hominins are known as
questions.a: tool makers

questions.q: Tools are sometimes called extra-corporal limbs because they
questions.a: work as extensions of the human body
o: work as extensions of the human body
are made of bone, like the limbs of the body
were worn on the legs to help early humans walk
grew on the body like natural limbs

questions.q: The earliest human settlements were found in Africa, Asia and Europe, together called the
questions.a: Old World

questions.a: are major evidence for reconstructing how ancestors lived
o: are major evidence for reconstructing how ancestors lived
prove nothing about the past, since they cannot be dated
show only the weather of the past and nothing about people
are used as money in the villages of the present

questions.q: Why did the making of stone tools mark the beginning of human behaviour, as opposed to animal behaviour?
questions.a: Animals do not have the cognitive ability to make tools. Our ancestors made, used and discarded tools, showing planning and skill.
s: Animals lack the ability to make tools

questions.q: The earliest stone tools were made about
questions.a: 3.3 million years ago

questions.q: Homo erectus made handaxes and ____.
questions.a: cleavers

questions.q: Homo habilis lived especially in
questions.a: the Olduvai Gorge in Africa
o: the Ganga plains, in the north of India
the Nile delta, in the north of Egypt
the Andes mountains, in South America

questions.q: When did the two major waves of human movement out of Africa take place, and by whom?
questions.a: About 2 million years ago by Homo erectus (spreading between 2 and 0.5 million years ago), and about 125,000 years ago by early Homo sapiens.
s: Homo erectus about 2 million years ago
Early Homo sapiens about 125,000 years ago

questions.q: What can skulls of early humans and modern humans tell us?
questions.a: Skulls show changes in shape and features from Homo habilis to Homo sapiens, such as a gradual straightening of the face, showing evolution.
s: Gradual straightening of the face or evolution

questions.q: How do we know that Homo erectus originated in Africa and spread to other continents?
questions.a: Handaxes and cleavers made by Homo erectus are found in Africa and also in parts of Asia and Europe. This shows they started in Africa and spread beyond it between 2 and 0.5 million years ago.
s: Similar tools found in Asia and Europe
Dispersal between 2 and 0.5 million years ago

questions.q: Different kinds of human ancestors
questions.a: co-existed at the same time
o: never lived together, since each kind replaced the earlier one
lived only in Asia, in the valleys of the great rivers
all made metal tools of copper and bronze

questions.q: What clues from discarded tools help archaeologists?
questions.a: Discarded tools were buried and later found by archaeologists. Finding similar tools in different places shows groups using similar techniques and how they lived.
s: Tools were buried and later discovered
They reveal how people lived and used objects

questions.q: Explain how Homo sapiens differ from earlier human ancestors according to the chapter.
questions.a: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago, moved out about 125,000 years ago and spread all over the earth. While all human ancestors were tool makers, Homo sapiens developed advanced technology and culture.

questions.q: Sam says humans first evolved in Australia. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The chapter says our earliest ancestors evolved and lived in Africa and later moved to other continents.

questions.q: Why do you think early humans left Africa? Give two possible reasons using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Changes in climate and environment may have made food scarce, and groups looking for new resources and habitats moved to other regions.

concepts.name: Palaeolithic and Mesolithic hunter-gatherers
concepts.description: The Stone Age stages, the Old Stone Age in the Indian subcontinent, the tools and art of hunter-gatherers and the Mesolithic changes.
concepts.idea: Hunter-gatherers made stone tools of increasing skill and, as the climate warmed, used small microlithic tools and fished.
concepts.rule: Stone Age: Palaeolithic (old stone), Mesolithic, Neolithic. Attirampakkam (1.5-1.7 million years) and Isampur (1.2 million years) have handaxes and cleavers. Later scrapers, borers, points, bow and arrow, blades. Mesolithic: microliths, fishing, population increase; Bhimbetka rock shelters.
concepts.example: Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu is dated to about 1.5-1.7 million years ago.

questions.q: The Stone Age is divided into
questions.a: Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic
o: Bronze, Iron and Copper, according to the metals used
Early, Middle and Late Harappan, according to the cities
Sumerian, Akkadian and Assyrian, according to the empires

questions.q: The word palaeolithic means
questions.a: old stone

questions.q: Attirampakkam is a Palaeolithic site in the state of ____.
questions.a: Tamil Nadu

questions.q: Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is known for
questions.a: hundreds of painted rock shelters
o: a great dockyard built of burnt bricks at the coast
granaries built to store grain for the whole city
step pyramids built as tombs for the kings

questions.a: chop meat, dig tubers, scrape skin and cleave bones
o: chop meat, dig tubers, scrape skin and cleave bones
plough fields and sow the seeds of wheat and barley
build brick houses and walls for the settlements
make pottery on a wheel for use in the villages

questions.a: scrapers, borers and points

questions.a: this made the small tools easier to use

stone could not be held in the hand at all

they were used only as decorations and beads

questions.a: became warmer, creating new environments and resources
o: became warmer, creating new environments and resources
became colder and covered the Earth with ice again
stayed the same as it had been for many thousands of years
became dry everywhere and turned all the land to desert

questions.q: Why did the population increase in the Mesolithic period?
questions.a: The warmer climate created forests and grasslands with more small game, fish and wild grains, so more food was available and population grew.
s: More food resources such as fish and grains

questions.q: Isampur in Karnataka is dated to about
questions.a: 1.2 million years ago

questions.q: A distinctive stone tool used to engrave symbols on bones and shells is a ____ (engraver).
questions.a: burin

questions.q: Which of these was invented by later hunter-gatherers?
questions.a: the bow and arrow

questions.q: Name two things Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers did that show symbolic communication.
questions.a: They decorated cave and rock shelter walls with paintings, used pigments to decorate their bodies, made beads of stone, bone and shell and engraved symbols on bones and shells.

questions.q: What tools were found at Attirampakkam and Isampur and what were they used for?
questions.a: Large cutting tools such as handaxes and cleavers, and stone scrapers and choppers made of quartzite and limestone. They were used to chop animal meat, dig out tubers, scrape animal skin and cleave bones.

questions.q: Describe the developments in tools and lifestyle between the early Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic period.
questions.a: Early Palaeolithic: large handaxes and cleavers. Later: smaller scrapers, borers, points, bow and arrow, blades. Mesolithic: microlithic tools, fishing and gathering aquatic food, more art and use of caves and rock shelters, and a population increase.

questions.q: Homo sapiens spread over Australia and the Americas between
questions.a: 50,000 and 12,000 years ago

questions.q: Why were hunter-gatherers able to hunt more efficiently with projectiles?
questions.a: They fitted stone points to their weapons so that they could be thrown or shot from a distance, which improved efficiency in hunting.
s: Hunting from a distance was more efficient

questions.q: Explain how the way of life of Mesolithic people differed from Palaeolithic people.
questions.a: Mesolithic people used small microlithic tools, gathered aquatic food and fishing became a mainstay, population grew, art flourished and caves and rock shelters were often occupied. Palaeolithic people relied more on large tools and hunting and gathering.

questions.q: Meera says Palaeolithic people grew crops in villages. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Palaeolithic people were hunter-gatherers. Farming and village settlements began in the Neolithic period.
s: Says they were hunter-gatherers and farming came later

questions.q: Fill a three-row table for Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic with one feature of tools and one of settlement each.
questions.a: Palaeolithic: handaxes, cleavers; wandering camps. Mesolithic: microliths; temporary settlements near rivers and lakes. Neolithic: tools for farming; permanent villages.

concepts.name: The Neolithic revolution and Mehrgarh
concepts.description: The shift from hunting and gathering to farming, the Neolithic period in the Indian subcontinent and Mehrgarh, and the Chalcolithic period.
concepts.idea: Domesticating plants and animals allowed people to settle in villages and make new tools and pottery.
concepts.rule: Neolithic revolution: domestication of animals and plants, tools for food production, pottery, first village settlements; it began at different times in different places. Mehrgarh (about 7000 BCE) is the oldest Neolithic site. Chalcolithic: use of copper with stone.
concepts.example: Mehrgarh people grew wheat and barley, raised sheep, goats and zebu cattle and made the first copper objects.

questions.q: The hallmark of the Neolithic revolution was
questions.a: the domestication of animals and plants
o: the domestication of animals and plants
the invention of writing and the use of scripts
the use of iron for tools and weapons
the building of pyramids and great temples

questions.q: Mehrgarh is located on the
questions.a: Bolan River

questions.q: Mehrgarh is the oldest ____ site in the Indian subcontinent.
questions.a: Neolithic

questions.q: Mehrgarh dates back to about
questions.a: 7000 BCE

questions.q: Neolithic farmers made tools for
questions.a: food production and processing
o: only hunting animals in the forests and grasslands
only fishing in the rivers and the sea
building ships to trade across the seas

questions.q: Neolithic communities established
questions.a: the first village settlements and made pottery
o: the first village settlements and made pottery
the first large empires, ruled by powerful kings
the first paper and the first books written on it
the first railways to carry grain to the cities

questions.q: The Neolithic revolution
questions.a: did not occur at the same time everywhere
o: did not occur at the same time everywhere
occurred everywhere on the same date in the same way
never occurred outside Africa, where it first began
ended farming and took people back to hunting

questions.q: The Chalcolithic period is the period of
questions.a: use of copper along with stone tools
o: use of copper along with stone tools
use of iron only, with no stone or copper tools
the Old Stone Age, when only stone tools were used
city-states, when writing and law had begun

questions.q: Why is the shift to farming called a revolution?
questions.a: It changed the way of life completely: people began to produce their own food, keep animals, settle in permanent villages and make new tools and pottery, laying the foundation for civilisation.
s: A complete change in food production and settled life
Led to villages, pottery or later civilisation

questions.q: The people of Mehrgarh cultivated
questions.a: wheat and barley

questions.q: Mehrgarh people raised sheep, goats and Indian cattle, especially the zebu ____ bull.
questions.a: humped

questions.q: Mehrgarh people were the first to make
questions.a: copper objects

questions.q: Name two features of the village settlement at Mehrgarh.
questions.a: Handmade sun-dried brick houses and granaries, graves for the dead, and ornaments of semi-precious stones and shells.

questions.q: What characterised the Neolithic way of life by 2500 BCE in the subcontinent?
questions.a: Herding of cattle, sheep and goats and cultivation of cereals, millets and pulses, sometimes interacting with Chalcolithic cultures.
s: Cultivation of cereals, millets and pulses

questions.q: Describe the Neolithic settlement of Mehrgarh.
questions.a: It was on the Bolan River and dates to about 7000 BCE. People built sun-dried brick houses and granaries, buried their dead, made ornaments of lapis lazuli, carnelian and shells, grew wheat and barley and raised sheep, goats and zebu, and were the first to make copper objects.

questions.q: Mehrgarh laid the basis for
questions.a: the Bronze Age Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation
o: the Egyptian pyramids, built along the Nile
the Great Wall, built in the north of China
the Roman empire, which grew around the Mediterranean

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the transition to farming happened at different times in different regions?
questions.a: Different regions had different climates, plants and animals, so hunter-gatherers there learned to domesticate them at different periods.

questions.q: Compare the tools and lifestyle of hunter-gatherers with Neolithic farmers.
questions.a: Hunter-gatherers made tools to procure food and moved to find it. Neolithic farmers made tools for food production and processing, made pottery, kept domesticated animals and plants and lived in permanent villages.

questions.q: Ali says farming made life easier in every way for early people. Evaluate.
questions.a: Not entirely. Farming gave surplus food and settled life but also brought new challenges such as dependence on weather, floods and the hard work of tending crops and animals.

questions.q: Imagine you are a Neolithic farmer at Mehrgarh. Describe one day of your life and one challenge.
questions.a: I wake in a mud-brick house, tend the wheat and barley fields, feed the sheep and goats and store grain in the granary. A challenge is a poor rainy season that damages the crop.

concepts.name: The Early Harappan phase and foundations of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation
concepts.description: Copper and early urban growth, continuity in crafts, farming, weights and measures and water management that led to the mature civilisation.
concepts.idea: Craft, farming, trade and water management developed step by step in the Early Harappan period.
concepts.rule: The civilisation emerged by 2600 BCE. Early Harappan continuity: pottery, beads, shell bangles, copper working; perimeter walls, seals and script beginnings. Kalibangan furrows show double cropping. Weights: binary multiples for small units, multiples of ten for larger. Water: gabarbands, Dholavira tanks, Lothal dockyard.
concepts.example: The Lothal dockyard was built entirely of burnt bricks.

questions.q: The Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation emerged by about
questions.a: 2600 BCE

questions.q: The Harappan dockyard at Lothal was built of
questions.a: burnt bricks

questions.q: The check dams built by Early Harappans across small streams are called ____.
questions.a: gabarbands

questions.q: The elaborate water harvesting system with tanks is at
questions.a: Dholavira

questions.q: Introduction of copper tools in the Indus and Ghaggar-Sarasvati plains
questions.a: increased productivity and prosperity
o: ended farming, since tools were no longer needed
stopped trade between the villages and the towns
destroyed pottery, which was replaced by copper vessels

questions.q: Ploughed fields at Kalibangan with horizontal and vertical furrows suggest
questions.a: double crop cultivation

questions.q: The Harappans used which system for weighing smaller units?
questions.a: a binary multiple system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16)
o: multiples of seven, such as 7, 14, 21 and 28
no system at all, since each trader used his own
a base 60 system, like that of the Sumerians

questions.q: Early Harappan graffiti on pottery and simple seals could be forerunners of
questions.a: the script and inscribed seals of the mature civilisation
o: the script and inscribed seals of the mature civilisation
iron tools and weapons of the later period
pyramids built for the rulers of the cities
the Great Wall built for the defence of the state

questions.q: Why were standard weights and measures important for the Harappans?
questions.a: They supported planned settlements and efficient trade between regions. Without a common system long-distance trade would have been difficult.
s: Standard system needed for planning or exchange

questions.q: Bhirrana and Kunal are sites where
questions.a: the Pre-Harappan phase is dated as early as 7000-5500 BCE
o: the Pre-Harappan phase is dated as early as 7000-5500 BCE
pyramids were built for the kings of the region
cuneiform was invented on clay tablets
the Great Wall was started against the raids of tribes

questions.q: Harappans used multiples of ____ for larger weights.
questions.a: ten

questions.q: Which craft was one of the major products that boosted the Early Harappan economy?
questions.a: pottery

questions.q: Name two crafts of Early Harappan people.
questions.a: Pottery, copper work, shell work (shell bangles), and production of semi-precious stone beads.

questions.q: What does the ploughed field at Kalibangan tell us?
questions.a: Its horizontal and vertical furrows show double crop cultivation, like the seasonal rabi and kharif cultivation still practised today, a tradition nearly 5000 years old.

questions.q: Describe the water management of the Harappans, giving three examples.
questions.a: Early Harappans built check dams called gabarbands across small streams to improve irrigation. At Dholavira water from two streams was diverted by dams and canals into a series of deep tanks cut into rock. The dockyard at Lothal was built of burnt bricks.

questions.q: The Early Harappan stage is described as showing
questions.a: cultural continuity into the mature civilisation
o: cultural continuity into the mature civilisation
a complete break with earlier cultures and their crafts
no crafts at all, only farming and herding
the use of iron in place of copper and stone

questions.q: How does the Early Harappan phase show continuity with the mature civilisation?
questions.a: Pottery traditions, semi-precious stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta objects and copper working continued, and perimeter walls, seals and the script probably began in this phase.

questions.q: Explain how technology and economic integration in the Early Harappan period led to urban centres.
questions.a: Copper tools raised productivity, pottery and other crafts and standard weights and measures supported trade between regions, and water management improved farming. These advances and economic links led to the rise of the urban centres of the mature civilisation.
s: Crafts and trade with standard measures

questions.q: Tara says the Harappan civilisation appeared suddenly with no earlier stages. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. It grew out of Neolithic and Early Harappan communities with continuity in crafts, farming and technology.
s: Refers to earlier stages or continuity

questions.q: Suggest how weights and measures might help a Harappan merchant travelling to a distant city.
questions.a: A standard system lets the merchant and buyer agree on quantities and prices, avoids disputes and makes long-distance trade reliable across regions.

concepts.name: The Mesopotamian civilisation
concepts.description: The river-valley civilisations, Mesopotamia and its city-states, the Sumerians and their writing, the Akkadian, Assyrian and Babylonian empires and contact with the Harappans.
concepts.idea: Mesopotamia produced the earliest city-based civilisation, with writing, temples, laws and trade.
concepts.rule: Four early river civilisations: Harappan, Mesopotamian, Egyptian and Chinese. Mesopotamia means land in between (Euphrates and Tigris). Sumerians: ziggurats, canals, cuneiform, base 60. Akkadian empire (Sargon), Assyrians, Babylon (Hammurabi and his code). Meluhha is identified with the Harappan civilisation.
concepts.example: The Code of Hammurabi served as a model for many later legal systems.

questions.q: Mesopotamia means
questions.a: the land in between

questions.q: Mesopotamia lies between the rivers
questions.a: Euphrates and Tigris

questions.a: cuneiform

questions.q: The temple tower of a Sumerian city is called a

questions.q: The Sumerians were the first to
questions.a: build dams and canals for irrigation and use mud and burnt bricks
o: build dams and canals for irrigation and use mud and burnt bricks
build the Great Wall to keep out the nomadic tribes
invent paper and write on it with brushes
write in Brahmi on the walls of their temples

pens on paper made from the bark of trees

chisels on bones and tortoise shells only

Meluhha in Akkadian records is generally identified with

Rome, the city on the banks of the Tiber

questions.q: Why were temples and ziggurats central to Sumerian cities?
questions.a: Each city built a grand temple for its chief god and the city grew around it. All economic activities such as agriculture, trade and transport were tied to the temple authority.
s: Economic activities tied to the temple

questions.q: The Code of Hammurabi is a
questions.a: compilation of rules and regulations for civil and social conduct
o: compilation of rules and regulations for civil and social conduct
set of religious hymns sung in the temples of the city
record of trade routes between Babylon and other cities
map of Babylon and the lands around it

questions.a: Babylonia

questions.a: the 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle

zero as a digit, used in the place value system

questions.q: Name the four major city-based civilisations of Mesopotamia in order of appearance.
questions.a: Sumerian, Akkadian, Assyrian and Babylonian.

questions.q: What did the Harappans trade with Mesopotamia, according to Akkadian records?
questions.a: Semi-precious stone beads, ivory, timber, gold dust and probably copper, through Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman).
s: Route or trading partners such as Dilmun and Magan

questions.q: Describe the achievements of the Sumerians.
questions.a: They built dams and canals and used mud and burnt bricks. They built ziggurats. They invented cuneiform writing around 3200 BCE, the wheeled cart and sailboat, and a number system based on 60 giving the 60-minute hour, 60-second minute and 360-degree circle.
s: Wheeled cart, sailboat or number system

questions.q: Why was there strong contact between Mesopotamia and the Harappans?
questions.a: They were geographically closer to each other than to Egypt or China
o: They were geographically closer to each other than to Egypt or China
They spoke the same language and wrote in the same script
They were ruled by one king who lived in Mesopotamia
They shared one script, which is now fully deciphered

questions.q: Why was Hammurabi important?
questions.a: He expanded Babylonia into a large empire and compiled the Code of Hammurabi, rules for civil and social conduct across his empire, which became a model for many later legal systems.
s: Code of laws as a model

questions.q: Explain why the Babylonian empire lost its prominence by 1400 BCE.
questions.a: Repeated attacks by the Hittites and other rising powers who mastered new technologies, along with environmental degradation, pressure on agricultural lands and internal political and economic problems, weakened Babylonian control.

questions.q: Sam says the four river civilisations all traded directly with each other. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Mesopotamia and the Harappans had strong contact because they were close, but Egypt and China have little tangible evidence of direct contact with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation.
s: Mentions Mesopotamia-Harappan contact but little for Egypt or China

questions.q: Suggest two ways a Sumerian priest and a scribe were important to the city.
questions.a: Priests led worship at the ziggurat and managed the temple economy. Scribes wrote records of farming and craft activities and laws on clay tablets, which kept the city organised.

concepts.name: The Egyptian civilisation
concepts.description: Egypt along the Nile, its calendar, writing and the deciphering of hieroglyphs, pharaohs and pyramids, society and daily life.
concepts.idea: The Nile's yearly flood gave Egypt fertile land, a calendar and a state ruled by pharaohs.
concepts.rule: Egyptians called their land Kemet (the black). City-states around 3000 BCE; the Nile flooded yearly. Calendar: 365 days (12 months of 30 days plus 5). Rosetta Stone found in 1799, deciphered by Champollion in 1822. Pharaohs, mastabas and pyramids (Saqqara step pyramid), belief in ka and mummification.
concepts.example: The Egyptian women could own property and run businesses; Cleopatra became queen at eighteen.

questions.q: The Egyptian civilisation grew along the river
questions.a: Nile

questions.q: Egyptians called their land Kemet, meaning
questions.a: the black land

questions.q: The rulers of Egypt were called ____.
questions.a: pharaohs

questions.q: The stone that helped decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs is the
questions.a: Rosetta Stone

questions.a: left rich fertile mud (kemet) on the land

questions.q: How did the Egyptians use the Nile's floods to develop a calendar?
questions.a: By counting the days between Nile floods the Egyptians developed a calendar based also on the rising of Sirius, with three seasons of four months.

questions.a: mastabas placed one on top of another

questions.a: papyrus

questions.q: Who deciphered the Egyptian script in 1822?
questions.a: Jean-Francois Champollion

questions.q: Who found the Rosetta Stone and when, and why was it a breakthrough?
questions.a: Pierre Bouchard found it in 1799. It had three types of writing including Greek, which people could read, so it was like a bilingual dictionary for the lost script.
s: Greek text helped decipher the script

questions.q: Name two rights or roles of Egyptian women.
questions.a: They could own property and run businesses, and had more rights than Greek or Roman women. Cleopatra was trained to rule and became queen at eighteen.
s: A second right or the example of Cleopatra

questions.q: Describe how pharaohs were buried and why pyramids were built.
questions.a: Pharaohs were buried deep underground with a rectangular structure called a mastaba over the burial chamber. Mastabas were stacked to form pyramids like the step pyramid at Saqqara. The Egyptians believed each person had a ka that lived on if the body was preserved by mummification.

questions.q: Digging ditches and building dams needed
questions.a: collective effort, which led to local government
o: collective effort, which led to local government
no cooperation, since each farmer did his own digging
only one person, who did all the work for the village
foreign help, since Egyptians had no skill in building

questions.q: How did the need for irrigation lead to the growth of government in Egypt?
questions.a: Digging ditches, reservoirs and dams needed collective effort, which led to organisation and an administrative class, probably the earliest form of local government.
s: This led to administration or local government

questions.q: Explain how the Nile helped the growth of Egyptian civilisation.
questions.a: The annual flood watered and enriched the land with black mud, so farming flourished. Farmers dug ditches and reservoirs, and counting the days between floods gave a calendar. Cooperation led to government, and the river was a route for movement.

questions.q: Ravi says Egyptian civilisation had no written records. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Egypt has rich records on papyrus and in hieroglyphs, deciphered using the Rosetta Stone, and Greek writers like Herodotus also wrote about Egypt.

questions.q: Describe two festivals or leisure activities of early Egyptians and what they show.
questions.a: Each god had a festival with the statue paraded with music (sistrum), and the Sed festival marked a king's 30th year. People also swam, canoed, played board games and enjoyed music and dancing. These show reverence for gods and the pharaoh and a rich social life.

concepts.name: The Chinese civilisation and the common features of Bronze Age civilisations
concepts.description: The Chinese civilisation along the Huang He and Yangtze, its dynasties, script and crafts, and what the early river civilisations share.
concepts.idea: Early civilisations grew independently in fertile river valleys and shared features such as farming, cities, writing and organised government.
concepts.rule: Chinese Neolithic cultures about 7000 BCE; bronze from about 2000 BCE; Shang (1600-1046 BCE), Zhou (1046-256 BCE), Qin (221-206 BCE), Han (206 BCE-220 CE). Oracle bones are the earliest source. Great Wall, jade, silk and the Silk Route. All four civilisations rose in river plains.
concepts.example: The name China probably comes from the Qin dynasty.

questions.q: The Chinese civilisation flourished along the rivers
questions.a: Huang He (Yellow River) and Yangtze
o: Nile and Congo, in the continent of Africa
Indus and Ganga, in the Indian subcontinent
Tigris and Euphrates, in western Asia

questions.q: The name China probably comes from the
questions.a: Qin dynasty

questions.q: The earliest sources of information about China are the oracle bones made of animal bones and ____ shells.
questions.a: tortoise

made of wedge-shaped marks pressed on clay tablets

based on pictures of animals only, with no other signs

questions.q: Silk became a major item of external trade during the
questions.a: Han dynasty

questions.q: Jade was valued in China because it
questions.a: was not locally available and was used for ritual and prestige objects
o: was not locally available and was used for ritual and prestige objects

questions.q: Which of these did China first introduce to the world?
questions.a: paper currency

questions.q: Why was the Great Wall built and over what period?
questions.a: It was built to protect against violent raids of nomadic tribes. Several walls were built from 680 BCE onwards and later joined, and expansion and repair continued till the 17th century CE.
s: Built over a long period from 680 BCE

questions.q: Name two Chinese dynasties and one feature of each.
questions.a: Shang (1600-1046 BCE): a Bronze Age dynasty. Zhou (1046-256 BCE): kings were also priests. Qin (221-206 BCE): unified China, the first imperial dynasty. Han (206 BCE-220 CE): silk trade grew.

questions.q: How do the oracle bones give information about early China?
questions.a: Symbols were written on animal bones and tortoise shells, which were heated until they cracked and the cracks interpreted to foretell the future. Today they tell about the hopes, desires and fears of early Chinese.
s: They tell about the people's hopes and fears

questions.q: Describe Chinese craft and trade achievements mentioned in the chapter.
questions.a: Jade carving including musical jade pieces, bronze weapons, tools and vessels, silk which became an important trade item on the Silk Route, and a money economy with metal-based exchange and later paper currency.

questions.q: Four early civilisations emerged in river plains: the Harappan, Mesopotamian, Egyptian and
questions.a: Chinese

questions.q: Why were rivers important in the growth of early civilisations?
questions.a: Rivers provided water for irrigation and fertile alluvial soil for farming, which gave surplus food, supported cities and trade and allowed transport.
s: Water and fertile soil for farming

questions.q: "Bronze Age civilisations developed independently but shared common features." Explain with examples.
questions.a: Each grew in a river valley (Sindhu-Sarasvati, Euphrates-Tigris, Nile, Huang He) with agriculture, urban centres, trade, social hierarchy, administration and writing systems such as Harappan script, cuneiform, hieroglyphs and Chinese characters, though they developed separately.
s: Cities, trade and hierarchy or administration

questions.q: Nita says all four early civilisations were in direct contact with one another. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. They emerged independently; Mesopotamia and the Harappans were in contact, but there is little evidence that Egypt or China had direct contact with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation.
s: Says they emerged independently with limited contact

questions.q: Prepare three points comparing Egypt and Mesopotamia: one on rivers, one on writing and one on religion or rulers.
questions.a: Rivers: Egypt on the Nile, Mesopotamia on the Euphrates and Tigris. Writing: hieroglyphs on papyrus versus cuneiform on clay. Rulers and religion: pharaohs and pyramids versus city-states with ziggurat temples.
